## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!TIP]
> **Rapid Revision Checklist — Small Signal Voltage Gain**

- [x] **Two-stage analysis is mandatory:** DC analysis (find Q-point) → AC analysis (compute $A_v$).
- [x] **The small-signal condition:** $\vert v_{be}\vert \le 10\,\text{mV}$ for BJT; signal is a perturbation around the Q-point.
- [x] **Thermal voltage** $V_T = 26\,\text{mV}$ at 300 K (room temperature).
- [x] **Transconductance** $g_m = I_C / V_T$ — the most important small-signal parameter.
- [x] **Base-emitter resistance** $r_\pi = \beta / g_m$ — same as $h_{ie}$ in CE h-parameters.
- [x] **CE gain formula:** $A_v \approx -g_m R_L'$ — **negative sign** = 180° phase inversion.
- [x] **CB gain formula:** $A_v \approx +g_m R_L'$ — **no inversion**, but very low input impedance.
- [x] **CC gain formula:** $A_v \approx 1$ — unity gain, used as a buffer (emitter follower).
- [x] **FET CS gain:** $A_v = -g_m (R_D \vert\vert R_L)$ — same form as BJT CE.
- [x] **Unbypassed $R_E$** reduces gain to $A_v \approx -R_L'/R_E$ but stabilizes the operating point and improves linearity (negative feedback).
- [x] **Always compute $R_L' = R_C \vert\vert R_L$** (or $R_D \vert\vert R_L$ for FETs) — do NOT use $R_C$ alone if a load is present.
- [x] **$A_{vs} \ne A_v$:** Overall source-to-output gain includes the input voltage divider: $A_{vs} = A_v \cdot r_\pi / (R_S + r_\pi)$.
- [x] **Decibel conversion:** $A_v (\text{dB}) = 20 \log_{10}\vert A_v\vert$.
- [x] **Phase inversion is a feature, not a bug:** The CE/CS amplifier is inherently an inverter. If a non-inverting amplifier is needed, use a CB/CG, CC/CD, or a two-stage CE cascade (which gives an in-phase output since two inversions = no inversion).
- [x] **KTU 2024 emphasis:** The Module 2 questions frequently combine h-parameter model derivation with a numerical computation (DC bias + $g_m$ + $A_v$ + $A_{vs}$), so practice both **derivation** and **numerical problem-solving** types.

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

topics.title: Input and Output Impedance
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME** > - **Course:** PCECT303 - ANALOG CIRCUITS > - **Module:** Module 2 > - **Topic:** Input and Output Impedance # SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview ## 1.1 Formal Definition of Input Impedance ($Z_{in}$) The **Input Impedance** of a two-port network (or amplifier) is defined as the impedance measured at the input terminals (port 1) with the output terminals (port 2) connected to the rated load $Z_L$ and the input source applied. Mathematically, it is the ratio of the input port voltage to the input port current, looking into the network from the source side: $$Z_{in} = \frac{V_{in}}{I_{in}}\bigg|_{V_{out} \text{ loaded}}$$ For purely resistive circuits, it is called **Input Resistance ($R_{in}$)**. The unit is the **Ohm ($\Omega$)**. > [!IMPORTANT] > **KTU 2024 Syllabus Note:** A high input impedance is always desirable in voltage amplifiers so that the amplifier does not "load down" the preceding stage or the signal source, thereby drawing minimal current and preserving the source signal's amplitude. ## 1.2 Formal Definition of Output Impedance ($Z_{out}$) The **Output Impedance** is defined as the equivalent Thevenin impedance looking back into the output terminals of the network with the input source deactivated (independent voltage sources short-circuited and independent current sources open-circuited) and the load $Z_L$ removed. $$Z_{out} = \frac{V_{oc}}{I_{sc}}\bigg|_{V_s = 0, Z_L \text{ removed}}$$ > [!NOTE] > **Key Concept:** A low output impedance is desirable so that the amplifier can drive low-impedance loads without significant signal attenuation, acting almost as an ideal voltage source. ## 1.3 Conceptual Analogy — The "Water Tap and Pipe" Model Imagine a water tank supplying water to your house: - **Input Impedance** is like the **diameter of the inlet pipe** of the tank. If the inlet pipe is very narrow (low $Z_{in}$), the water source (city pump) has to work very hard, and pressure drops. A wide inlet (high $Z_{in}$) means the tank easily accepts water without disturbing the source. - **Output Impedance** is like the **friction inside the outlet pipe** of the tank. If the outlet pipe has high friction (high $Z_{out}$), the water flow at the tap reduces significantly when you open the tap (connect a load). A low-friction pipe (low $Z_{out}$) ensures the water flow at the tap remains nearly constant, no matter how much you open it. In short: **High $Z_{in}$, Low $Z_{out}$** is the design goal of a near-ideal **Voltage Amplifier**. ## 1.4 Role in Cascaded Amplifier Systems In a multi-stage amplifier, the input impedance of stage 2 acts as the load for stage 1, and the output impedance of stage 1 acts as the source for stage 2. This forms the basis of the **"loading effect"** that KTU examiners love to test in numerical problems. > [!TIP] > **Golden Rule of Cascading:** The overall voltage gain is **not** simply the product of individual stage gains. The actual gain is reduced due to loading: $A_{v,\text{actual}} = A_{v1} \cdot \frac{Z_{in2}}{Z_{in2} + Z_{out1}} \cdot A_{v2}$. # SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet ## 2.1 Why Are $Z_{in}$ and $Z_{out}$ So Important? 1. **Maximum Power Transfer:** When the load impedance equals the complex conjugate of the source impedance ($Z_L = Z_s^*$), maximum power is delivered. This is critical in RF and communication circuits. 2. **Loading Effect / Signal Integrity:** Mismatched impedances cause voltage division between stages, reducing gain. 3. **Bandwidth Considerations:** Input and output impedances, combined with shunt/series capacitances (Miller effect), determine the **3-dB cutoff frequencies** of the amplifier. ## 2.2 Standard Two-Port Network Framework For a linear two-port network, the standard hybrid-parameter (h-parameter) and the g-parameter models are widely used. For low-frequency small-signal analysis: | Parameter | Definition | Physical Meaning | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | $h_{11}$ | $V_1 / I_1 \vert_{V_2=0}$ | Input impedance with output shorted ($h_{ie} \approx r_\pi$) | | $h_{12}$ | $V_1 / V_2 \vert_{I_1=0}$ | Reverse voltage ratio (feedback) | | $h_{21}$ | $I_2 / I_1 \vert_{V_2=0}$ | Forward current gain ($\beta$ or $h_{fe}$) | | $h_{22}$ | $I_2 / V_2 \vert_{I_1=0}$ | Output admittance ($1/r_o$) | ## 2.3 BJT Amplifier Configurations — $Z_{in}$ and $Z_{out}$ Summary For a BJT with small-signal parameters $r_\pi$, $\beta$, $g_m$, $r_o$ and source resistance $R_S$: | Configuration | Input Impedance $Z_{in}$ | Output Impedance $Z_{out}$ | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Common Emitter (CE) | $R_B \parallel r_\pi$ | $R_C \parallel r_o$ | | Common Base (CB) | $R_E \parallel \dfrac{r_\pi}{\beta+1} \approx \dfrac{1}{g_m}$ | $R_C \parallel r_o$ | | Common Collector (CC) | $R_B \parallel \left[r_\pi + (\beta+1)R_E'\right]$ | $R_E \parallel \dfrac{r_\pi + R_S'\vert\beta+1}{\beta+1}$ | | Emitter Degenerated CE | $R_B \parallel \left[r_\pi + (\beta+1)R_E\right]$ | $\approx R_C$ (when $R_E$ bypassed only) | > [!NOTE] > $R_E' = R_E \parallel R_L$ for AC analysis. $R_S' = R_S \parallel R_B$ for AC analysis. ## 2.4 FET Amplifier Configurations — $Z_{in}$ and $Z_{out}$ Summary | Configuration | Input Impedance $Z_{in}$ | Output Impedance $Z_{out}$ | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Common Source (CS) | $R_G \parallel (R_1 \parallel R_2)$ | $R_D \parallel r_d$ | | Common Drain (CD) | $R_G \parallel (R_1 \parallel R_2)$ | $R_S \parallel \dfrac{1}{g_m} \parallel r_d$ | | Common Gate (CG) | $R_S \parallel \dfrac{1}{g_m}$ | $R_D \parallel r_d$ | ## 2.5 KTU Formula Cheat Sheet | # | Formula | Description | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | 1 | $Z_{in} = \dfrac{V_{in}}{I_{in}}$ | Fundamental input impedance definition | | 2 | $Z_{out} = \left.\dfrac{V_{oc}}{I_{sc}}\right\vert_{V_s=0}$ | Fundamental output impedance definition | | 3 | $A_{v,\text{loaded}} = A_{v,\text{no-load}} \cdot \dfrac{Z_{in}}{Z_{in}+Z_S}$ | Loading effect on voltage gain | | 4 | $R_{in}(\text{CE}) = R_B \parallel r_\pi$ | CE configuration | | 5 | $R_{in}(\text{CC}) = R_B \parallel [r_\pi + (\beta+1)R_E']$ | Emitter Follower | | 6 | $R_{out}(\text{CC}) = R_E \parallel \dfrac{R_S'\vert\beta+1 + r_\pi}{\beta+1}$ | Approx. emitter follower output | | 7 | $R_{in}(\text{CB}) \approx \dfrac{1}{g_m}$ | Approx. for $r_o \to \infty$ | | 8 | $R_{in}(\text{CS}) = R_G$ | FET CS, assuming $R_G$ gate resistor | | 9 | $R_{out}(\text{CD}) = R_S \parallel \dfrac{1}{g_m}$ | Source follower output | | 10 | $Z_L = Z_S^*$ | Maximum power transfer condition | ## 2.6 Real-World Engineering Utility - **Audio Preamplifiers:** Require very high $Z_{in}$ ($\geq 500\text{ k}\Omega$) to avoid loading piezoelectric microphones. - **Operational Amplifiers:** The ideal op-amp model has $Z_{in} = \infty$ and $Z_{out} = 0$. Real op-amps (e.g., LM741, TL081) approach these values. - **Antenna Systems:** Impedance matching ($50\ \Omega$ standard) between transmitter, cable, and antenna is critical for SWR (Standing Wave Ratio). - **Instrumentation:** High $Z_{in}$ voltmeters (FET input) prevent loading of the circuit under test. # SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix ## 3.1 Derivation of $Z_{in}$ for Common Emitter (CE) Amplifier with Bypass Capacitor **Given Circuit:** BJT in CE configuration with base bias resistors $R_1$, $R_2$, emitter resistor $R_E$ fully bypassed by $C_E$, collector resistor $R_C$, and load $R_L$ at the output through coupling capacitor $C_{c2}$. **Step 1 — Replace the BJT with its small-signal hybrid-$\pi$ model.** The base node connects to $r_\pi$ between base and emitter, and the emitter is grounded (because $C_E$ short-circuits $R_E$ at AC). The collector connects to $R_C \parallel R_L$ at AC, in parallel with $r_o$. **Step 2 — Apply KCL at the input node (base).** The current $I_b$ flows into the base. The total input current $I_{in}$ splits between the bias network and the BJT base: $$I_{in} = I_{R_B} + I_b$$ where $R_B = R_1 \parallel R_2$ is the Thevenin equivalent of the base bias network. **Step 3 — Express input voltage $V_{in}$.** $V_{in}$ is the voltage at the base node. The voltage across $r_\pi$ is $V_\pi = I_b \cdot r_\pi$. Since the emitter is AC-grounded: $$V_{in} = I_b \cdot r_\pi$$ **Step 4 — Substitute into the input impedance formula.** $$Z_{in} = \frac{V_{in}}{I_{in}} = \frac{V_{in}}{I_{R_B} + I_b} = \frac{V_{in}}{\frac{V_{in}}{R_B} + \frac{V_{in}}{r_\pi}}$$ Factoring $V_{in}$ out: $$Z_{in} = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{R_B} + \frac{1}{r_\pi}}$$ Therefore: $$\boxed{Z_{in} = R_B \parallel r_\pi}$$ This is the standard result. If $R_B \gg r_\pi$ (typical case), then $Z_{in} \approx r_\pi$. --- ## 3.2 Derivation of $Z_{out}$ for Common Emitter (CE) Amplifier **Step 1 — Deactivate the independent source.** To find $Z_{out}$, set $V_s = 0$ (short the input voltage source). This means the base is AC-grounded through $R_S' = R_S \parallel R_B$. **Step 2 — Apply a test voltage $V_{test}$ at the output node.** Connect a fictitious test source $V_{test}$ at the output terminals (where $R_L$ was connected). Compute the resulting current $I_{test}$ flowing into the output. **Step 3 — Find the current $I_{test}$.** With the base AC-grounded, $V_\pi = 0$, which means the dependent current source $g_m V_\pi = 0$ (open circuit). The only path for $I_{test}$ is through $R_C$ and $r_o$ in parallel: $$I_{test} = \frac{V_{test}}{R_C} + \frac{V_{test}}{r_o}$$ **Step 4 — Compute the output impedance.** $$Z_{out} = \frac{V_{test}}{I_{test}} = \frac{V_{test}}{\frac{V_{test}}{R_C} + \frac{V_{test}}{r_o}} = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{R_C} + \frac{1}{r_o}}$$ Therefore: $$\boxed{Z_{out} = R_C \parallel r_o}$$ For an ideal Early-voltage-infinite BJT ($r_o \to \infty$), $Z_{out} = R_C$. --- ## 3.3 Derivation of $Z_{out}$ for Emitter Follower (CC) — The Tricky One! **Step 1 — Test source method again, with the input source shorted.** The emitter is no longer at AC ground because the emitter resistor $R_E$ (which carries the output current) is in the circuit. **Step 2 — Apply $V_{test}$ at the emitter node.** The base is AC-grounded through $R_S' = R_S \parallel R_B$. The voltage at the emitter is $V_e = V_{test}$. The voltage across $r_\pi$ is: $$V_\pi = V_b - V_e = 0 - V_{test} = -V_{test}$$ **Step 3 — The dependent current source delivers $g_m V_\pi = -g_m V_{test}$ from collector to emitter.** This current flows OUT of the emitter node (or rather, in a direction that adds to $I_{test}$). **Step 4 — Apply KCL at the emitter node.** The current $I_{test}$ flows into the emitter node and splits into three parallel paths: - Through $R_E$ (current $= V_{test}/R_E$) - Through $r_o$ (current $= V_{test}/r_o$) - Through the dependent source: total emitter current is $(\beta+1)I_b$ We need $I_b$ in terms of $V_{test}$: $$I_b = \frac{V_\pi}{r_\pi} = \frac{-V_{test}}{r_\pi}$$ The current through the BJT from emitter to collector is $(\beta+1)I_b = \dfrac{-(\beta+1)V_{test}}{r_\pi}$. **Step 5 — KCL gives:** $$I_{test} = \frac{V_{test}}{R_E} + \frac{V_{test}}{r_o} - \frac{(\beta+1)V_{test}}{r_\pi}$$ **Step 6 — Solve for $Z_{out}$:** $$Z_{out} = \frac{V_{test}}{I_{test}} = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{R_E} + \frac{1}{r_o} + \frac{\beta+1}{r_\pi}}$$ This is the parallel combination of $R_E$, $r_o$, and $\dfrac{r_\pi}{\beta+1} = \dfrac{1}{g_m}$: $$\boxed{Z_{out} = R_E \parallel r_o \parallel \frac{1}{g_m} = R_E \parallel r_o \parallel \frac{r_\pi}{\beta+1}}$$ > [!IMPORTANT] > The term $\dfrac{r_\pi}{\beta+1}$ is the resistance looking into the emitter, often denoted as $r_e$. This is the source of the very low output impedance of emitter followers. --- ## 3.4 Numerical Demonstration: Cascaded CE-CC Stage **Problem:** A CE stage has $R_S = 1\text{ k}\Omega$, $\beta = 100$, $r_\pi = 2.5\text{ k}\Omega$, $R_C = 4.7\text{ k}\Omega$. It drives an emitter follower with $R_E = 1\text{ k}\Omega$, $R_B = 100\text{ k}\Omega$. Find the overall loaded voltage gain if the input is $V_s = 10\text{ mV}$ and load $R_L = 1\text{ k}\Omega$. **Step 1 — CE Stage $Z_{in}$ (with biasing network assumed infinite for simplicity):** $$Z_{in,CE} = r_\pi = 2.5\text{ k}\Omega$$ **Step 2 — CE Stage $Z_{out}$:** $$Z_{out,CE} = R_C = 4.7\text{ k}\Omega$$ **Step 3 — CC Stage $Z_{in}$:** $$Z_{in,CC} = R_B \parallel [r_\pi + (\beta+1)(R_E \parallel R_L)]$$ Computing $R_E \parallel R_L = 1\text{k} \parallel 1\text{k} = 500\ \Omega$: $$r_\pi + 101 \times 500 = 2500 + 50500 = 53000\ \Omega = 53\text{ k}\Omega$$ $$Z_{in,CC} = 100\text{k} \parallel 53\text{k} = \frac{100 \times 53}{153} = 34.64\text{ k}\Omega$$ **Step 4 — CC Stage $Z_{out}$:** $$Z_{out,CC} = R_E \parallel \frac{r_\pi + (R_S \parallel R_B)}{\beta+1} = 1000 \parallel \frac{2500 + 1000}{101}$$ $$= 1000 \parallel \frac{3500}{101} = 1000 \parallel 34.65 = 33.5\ \Omega$$ **Step 5 — Overall loaded gain:** Gain of CE stage: $A_{v,CE} = -g_m (R_C \parallel Z_{in,CC}) = -\frac{100}{2500}(4700 \parallel 34640)$ $R_C \parallel Z_{in,CC} = \frac{4700 \times 34640}{39340} = 4138\ \Omega$ $$A_{v,CE} = -0.04 \times 4138 = -165.5$$ Gain of CC stage: $A_{v,CC} = \dfrac{(\beta+1)(R_E \parallel R_L)}{r_\pi + (\beta+1)(R_E \parallel R_L)} = \dfrac{101 \times 500}{53000} = 0.953$ Overall: $A_v = -165.5 \times 0.953 = -157.7$ The output voltage: $V_{out} = A_v \times V_{in}$. With the source loading, $V_{in} = V_s \times \dfrac{Z_{in,CE}}{Z_{in,CE}+R_S} = 10\text{mV} \times \dfrac{2.5}{3.5} = 7.14\text{ mV}$. $$V_{out} = -157.7 \times 7.14\text{ mV} = -1.126\text{ V}$$ > [!TIP] > The emitter follower provides a high $Z_{in}$ to the CE stage (preventing loading) and a low $Z_{out}$ to the load — a classic impedance transformation. # SECTION 4: Structural Diagrams & Schematics ## 4.1 Two-Port Network Block Diagram (Master Reference) ```mermaid graph LR srcA[Input Source Vs]:::src -->|Rs| port1A[Port 1
Input Terminals] port1A --> zinA[Zin Block]:::imp zinA --> ampCoreA[Amplification
Core with Av]:::amp ampCoreA --> zoutA[Zout Block]:::imp zoutA --> port2A[Port 2
Output Terminals] port2A --> loadA[Load ZL]:::ld classDef src fill:#FFD700,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef imp fill:#FF6347,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px,color:#FFF classDef amp fill:#4682B4,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px,color:#FFF classDef ld fill:#90EE90,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 ``` ## 4.2 Test Source Method for Output Impedance ```mermaid graph TD inpB[Input Port
Vs SHORTED]:::gnd --> ampInB[Amplifier
Internal]:::amp ampInB --> nodeB[Output Node]:::node nodeB --> zoutB[Zout = Vtest / Itest]:::imp zoutB --> vtestB[Test Voltage Vtest]:::src vtestB --> itestB[Test Current Itest]:::cur classDef gnd fill:#A9A9A9,stroke:#000,stroke-width:2px,color:#FFF classDef amp fill:#4682B4,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px,color:#FFF classDef node fill:#FFA500,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef imp fill:#FF6347,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px,color:#FFF classDef src fill:#FFD700,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef cur fill:#9370DB,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px,color:#FFF ``` ## 4.3 Cascaded Multi-Stage Architecture (Loading Effect Visualized) ```mermaid graph LR vsC[Source Vs with Rs]:::src --> stage1In[Stage 1 Input]:::node stage1In --> zin1C[Zin1]:::imp zin1C --> amp1C[Amplifier 1
Av1]:::amp amp1C --> zout1C[Zout1]:::imp zout1C --> stage2In[Stage 2 Input]:::node stage2In --> zin2C[Zin2]:::imp zin2C --> amp2C[Amplifier 2
Av2]:::amp amp2C --> zout2C[Zout2]:::imp zout2C --> loadC[Load ZL]:::ld note1C[/"Loading: Zout1 drives Zin2"/]:::note -.-> zin2C classDef src fill:#FFD700,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef imp fill:#FF6347,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px,color:#FFF classDef amp fill:#4682B4,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px,color:#FFF classDef node fill:#FFA500,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef ld fill:#90EE90,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef note fill:#FFE4B5,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px,color:#000 ``` ## 4.4 BJT Configuration Comparison Flow ```mermaid graph TD bjt[BJT Three Configurations]:::root --> ceN[Common Emitter CE]:::ce bjt --> cbN[Common Base CB]:::cb bjt --> ccN[Common Collector CC]:::cc ceN --> ceZin[Zin: Moderate to High
Rb parallel rpi]:::ce ceN --> ceZout[Zout: Moderate
Rc parallel ro]:::ce cbN --> cbZin[Zin: Very Low
approx 1 by gm]:::cb cbN --> cbZout[Zout: Moderate
Rc parallel ro]:::cb ccN --> ccZin[Zin: Very High
Rb parallel rb plus beta Re]:::cc ccN --> ccZout[Zout: Very Low
Re parallel 1 by gm]:::cc classDef root fill:#2F4F4F,stroke:#000,stroke-width:3px,color:#FFF classDef ce fill:#FFB6C1,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef cb fill:#B0E0E6,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef cc fill:#98FB98,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 ``` ## 4.5 Miller's Theorem and Input Capacitance Multiplication ```mermaid graph LR inNodeM[Input Node Vi]:::node --> cMulM[CMiller
equal to C times 1 minus Av]:::cap cMulM --> gndM[AC Ground]:::gnd outNodeM[Output Node Vo]:::node --> cOrigM[Corig
Internal Capacitance]:::cap cOrigM --> inNodeM noteM[/"Miller Effect multiplies
C by factor 1 plus Av"/]:::note -.-> cMulM classDef node fill:#FFA500,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef cap fill:#DDA0DD,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef gnd fill:#A9A9A9,stroke:#000,stroke-width:2px,color:#FFF classDef note fill:#FFE4B5,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px,color:#000 ``` # SECTION 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap ## 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each) ### Question 1: `[KTU University Exam - May 2024]` **Define input impedance and output impedance of an amplifier. Why is a high input impedance and low output impedance desirable for a voltage amplifier?** **Model Answer:** **Input Impedance ($Z_{in}$):** It is the impedance offered by the amplifier at its input terminals to the source signal. It is defined as the ratio of input voltage to input current: $Z_{in} = V_{in}/I_{in}$, with the output loaded. **Output Impedance ($Z_{out}$):** It is the Thevenin equivalent impedance looking back into the output terminals with the input source deactivated and the load removed. **Why High $Z_{in}$:** A high input impedance ensures the amplifier draws negligible current from the source, preventing signal attenuation and source loading. Mathematically, the voltage appearing at the input is $V_{in} = V_s \cdot Z_{in}/(Z_{in}+R_S)$. As $Z_{in} \to \infty$, $V_{in} \to V_s$ (no loss). **Why Low $Z_{out}$:** A low output impedance ensures the output voltage remains nearly constant irrespective of load variations, behaving like an ideal voltage source. The loaded gain becomes $A_{v,\text{loaded}} = A_{v,\text{no-load}} \cdot Z_L/(Z_L+Z_{out})$. As $Z_{out} \to 0$, the full no-load gain is delivered to the load. **(3 marks)** --- ### Question 2: `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]` **Compare the input and output impedances of Common Emitter (CE) and Common Collector (CC) configurations.** **Model Answer:** | Parameter | Common Emitter (CE) | Common Collector (CC) | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | $Z_{in}$ | Moderate: $R_B \parallel r_\pi$ | Very High: $R_B \parallel [r_\pi + (\beta+1)R_E']$ | | $Z_{out}$ | Moderate: $R_C \parallel r_o \approx R_C$ | Very Low: $R_E \parallel \dfrac{r_\pi + R_S'}{\beta+1}$ | **Explanation:** The CC (emitter follower) has high $Z_{in}$ because the emitter resistor $R_E$ is reflected back to the base multiplied by $(\beta+1)$. The CC has low $Z_{out}$ because the source resistance $R_S'$ when reflected to the emitter is divided by $(\beta+1)$. Therefore, the CC acts as an excellent **impedance buffer** between a high-impedance source and a low-impedance load. **(3 marks)** --- ## 5.2 Part B — 14-Mark Questions (Module Internal Choice Format) ### QUESTION A — `[KTU University Exam - May 2024, Module 2]` **(a) [7 Marks]** Derive the expression for the input impedance of a Common Emitter (CE) amplifier with an unbypassed emitter resistor $R_E$. Show that $Z_{in} = R_B \parallel [r_\pi + (\beta+1)R_E]$. **(b) [7 Marks]** A Common Source (CS) MOSFET amplifier has $g_m = 2\text{ mA/V}$, $r_d = 50\text{ k}\Omega$, $R_D = 10\text{ k}\Omega$, $R_S = 1\text{ k}\Omega$ (unbypassed), and gate bias resistors $R_1 = 1\text{ M}\Omega$, $R_2 = 500\text{ k}\Omega$. Find the input impedance, output impedance, and voltage gain. --- #### Model Solution for Question A(a): **Given:** CE amplifier with bias resistors $R_1$, $R_2$ (Thevenin equivalent $R_B$), emitter resistor $R_E$ (no bypass capacitor), collector resistor $R_C$, BJT with hybrid-$\pi$ parameters $r_\pi$, $\beta$, $r_o$. **Step 1 — Replace BJT with small-signal model.** The emitter is NOT AC-grounded now, so $R_E$ is in the circuit. **Step 2 — Apply a test voltage $V_{in}$ at the base and find the base current $I_b$.** The voltage across $r_\pi$ is $V_\pi = I_b \cdot r_\pi$. The voltage at the emitter is $V_e = (I_b + I_c) R_E = (I_b + \beta I_b) R_E = (\beta+1) I_b R_E$. **Step 3 — KVL around base-emitter loop:** $$V_{in} = V_\pi + V_e = I_b r_\pi + (\beta+1) I_b R_E = I_b [r_\pi + (\beta+1) R_E]$$ **Step 4 — Input impedance looking into the base alone:** $$Z_{b} = \frac{V_{in}}{I_b} = r_\pi + (\beta+1)R_E$$ **Step 5 — Include the bias network in parallel:** $$\boxed{Z_{in} = R_B \parallel [r_\pi + (\beta+1)R_E]}$$ **Physical Interpretation:** The unbypassed $R_E$ is "reflected" to the base as $(\beta+1)R_E$ due to the current amplification. This greatly increases input impedance but reduces voltage gain. **(7 marks)** --- #### Model Solution for Question A(b): **Step 1 — Compute Thevenin resistance of gate bias network:** $$R_G = R_1 \parallel R_2 = \frac{1\text{M} \times 500\text{k}}{1\text{M}+500\text{k}} = \frac{500}{1.5}\text{ k}\Omega = 333.33\text{ k}\Omega$$ **Step 2 — Input Impedance:** For a MOSFET, the gate draws no DC current. The input impedance is essentially the gate bias network: $$Z_{in} = R_1 \parallel R_2 = R_G = 333.33\text{ k}\Omega$$ **Step 3 — Output Impedance:** For a CS amplifier, the output looking into the drain is $r_d$. The total output impedance is $R_D$ in parallel with $r_d$: $$Z_{out} = R_D \parallel r_d = \frac{10\text{k} \times 50\text{k}}{10\text{k} + 50\text{k}} = \frac{500}{60}\text{ k}\Omega = 8.33\text{ k}\Omega$$ **Step 4 — Voltage Gain (with unbypassed $R_S$):** For a CS stage with source degeneration $R_S$: $$A_v = -\frac{g_m (R_D \parallel r_d \parallel R_L)}{1 + g_m R_S}$$ Assuming no external load ($R_L \to \infty$): $$A_v = -\frac{2\text{mA/V} \times 8.33\text{ k}\Omega}{1 + 2\text{mA/V} \times 1\text{ k}\Omega} = -\frac{16.66}{1+2} = -\frac{16.66}{3} = -5.55$$ $$\boxed{Z_{in} = 333.33\text{ k}\Omega, \quad Z_{out} = 8.33\text{ k}\Omega, \quad A_v = -5.55}$$ **(7 marks)** --- ### QUESTION B — Alternative Choice `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023, Module 2]` **(a) [7 Marks]** Explain the "test source method" for finding the output impedance of an amplifier. Apply this method to find the output impedance of an emitter follower with $R_S = 1\text{ k}\Omega$, $R_B = 100\text{ k}\Omega$, $R_E = 2\text{ k}\Omega$, $R_L = 5\text{ k}\Omega$, $\beta = 100$, $r_\pi = 2.5\text{ k}\Omega$. **(b) [7 Marks]** Two amplifier stages are cascaded. Stage 1 has $A_{v1} = 50$, $Z_{out1} = 5\text{ k}\Omega$. Stage 2 has $Z_{in2} = 20\text{ k}\Omega$, $A_{v2} = 30$. If the source has $R_S = 1\text{ k}\Omega$ and $Z_{in1} = 10\text{ k}\Omega$, find the overall voltage gain $A_v = V_{out}/V_s$ accounting for loading effects. --- #### Model Solution for Question B(a): **Test Source Method Explanation:** To find the output impedance of a network: 1. **Deactivate all independent sources:** Replace independent voltage sources with short circuits and independent current sources with open circuits. 2. **Remove the load** $R_L$ from the output terminals. 3. **Apply a fictitious test voltage source $V_{test}$** at the output terminals. 4. **Measure (or compute) the resulting test current $I_{test}$** flowing into the network from $V_{test}$. 5. **Output impedance is $Z_{out} = V_{test} / I_{test}$.** **Numerical Application — Emitter Follower:** **Step 1 — Deactivate the source:** $V_s$ shorted means base is AC-grounded through $R_S \parallel R_B$. $$R_S' = R_S \parallel R_B = \frac{1\text{k} \times 100\text{k}}{1\text{k}+100\text{k}} = \frac{100}{101} = 0.990\text{ k}\Omega = 990\ \Omega$$ **Step 2 — Apply $V_{test}$ at emitter. Find $V_\pi$:** $$V_\pi = V_b - V_e = 0 - V_{test} = -V_{test}$$ **Step 3 — The current entering the BJT from the emitter terminal is:** $$I_{bjt} = -(\beta+1) I_b = -(\beta+1) \cdot \frac{V_\pi}{r_\pi} = -101 \cdot \frac{-V_{test}}{2.5\text{k}} = \frac{101 V_{test}}{2500} = 40.4 \times 10^{-3} V_{test}$$ This represents the current flowing from the test source INTO the emitter of the BJT (in the model). **Step 4 — KCL at the emitter node:** $$I_{test} = I_{R_E} + I_{bjt} = \frac{V_{test}}{R_E} + \frac{(\beta+1)V_{test}}{r_\pi}$$ $$I_{test} = \frac{V_{test}}{2000} + \frac{101 V_{test}}{2500}$$ $$I_{test} = V_{test} \left(5 \times 10^{-4} + 40.4 \times 10^{-3}\right) = V_{test} \times 0.0409$$ **Step 5 — Output impedance:** $$Z_{out} = \frac{V_{test}}{I_{test}} = \frac{1}{0.0409} = 24.45\ \Omega$$ If we include the effect of $R_E' = R_E \parallel R_L = 2\text{k} \parallel 5\text{k} = 1.428\text{ k}\Omega$ when the load is reconnected, $Z_{out} \approx R_E \parallel \dfrac{r_\pi + R_S'}{\beta+1} = 2000 \parallel \dfrac{2500+990}{101} = 2000 \parallel 34.55 = 34.0\ \Omega$. $$\boxed{Z_{out} \approx 24.45\ \Omega \text{ (without load)}, \approx 34.0\ \Omega \text{ (with load reference)}}$$ This very low output impedance is the hallmark of the emitter follower. **(7 marks)** --- #### Model Solution for Question B(b): **Step 1 — Source-to-Stage 1 loading:** The voltage reaching the input of stage 1 is: $$V_{in1} = V_s \cdot \frac{Z_{in1}}{Z_{in1} + R_S} = V_s \cdot \frac{10\text{k}}{10\text{k}+1\text{k}} = \frac{10}{11} V_s = 0.909 V_s$$ **Step 2 — Stage 1 output to Stage 2 input loading:** The voltage at the input of stage 2 is the voltage at the output of stage 1, attenuated by the voltage divider formed by $Z_{out1}$ and $Z_{in2}$: $$V_{in2} = V_{out1} \cdot \frac{Z_{in2}}{Z_{in2} + Z_{out1}} = V_{out1} \cdot \frac{20\text{k}}{20\text{k}+5\text{k}} = \frac{20}{25} V_{out1} = 0.8 V_{out1}$$ **Step 3 — Output of stage 1:** $$V_{out1} = A_{v1} \cdot V_{in1} = 50 \cdot 0.909 V_s = 45.45 V_s$$ **Step 4 — Input and output of stage 2:** $$V_{in2} = 0.8 \times 45.45 V_s = 36.36 V_s$$ $$V_{out} = A_{v2} \cdot V_{in2} = 30 \times 36.36 V_s = 1090.9 V_s$$ **Step 5 — Overall voltage gain:** $$\boxed{A_v = \frac{V_{out}}{V_s} = 1090.9}$$ > [!WARNING] > **KTU Examiner's Pitfall Alert:** Many students naively compute $A_v = 50 \times 30 = 1500$ and lose **3 marks**. The correct answer of **1090.9** accounts for the loading effects at both the source-to-input interface and the inter-stage interface. The "no-load" gain of 1500 is a textbook fiction in real cascaded systems. **(7 marks)** --- ## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember > [!IMPORTANT] > **High-Density Revision Checklist for KTU 2024:** - $Z_{in}$ is measured at the input port with the **load connected** at the output; $Z_{out}$ is measured at the output port with the **input source deactivated** and load removed. - **Test source method** is the universal technique: apply $V_{test}$, find $I_{test}$, then $Z_{out} = V_{test}/I_{test}$. - **CE:** $Z_{in} = R_B \parallel r_\pi$; $Z_{out} = R_C \parallel r_o$. (Moderate both.) - **CB:** $Z_{in} \approx 1/g_m$ (very low); $Z_{out} = R_C \parallel r_o$. (Good for high-frequency, low-impedance sources.) - **CC (Emitter Follower):** $Z_{in} = R_B \parallel [r_\pi + (\beta+1)R_E']$ (very high); $Z_{out} = R_E \parallel r_\pi/(\beta+1)$ (very low). (Best impedance buffer.) - **CS (FET):** $Z_{in} = R_G$ (extremely high — ideal for high-impedance sources); $Z_{out} = R_D \parallel r_d$. - **CD (Source Follower):** $Z_{in} = R_G$; $Z_{out} = R_S \parallel 1/g_m$ (low). - **Unbypassed $R_E$** in CE reflects to base as $(\beta+1)R_E$, boosting $Z_{in}$ but reducing $A_v$ by factor $(1+g_m R_E)$. - **Loading effect** in cascaded stages: $A_{v,\text{overall}} = A_{v1} \cdot \dfrac{Z_{in2}}{Z_{in2}+Z_{out1}} \cdot A_{v2} \cdot \dfrac{Z_L}{Z_L+Z_{out2}}$. - **Maximum power transfer** condition: $Z_L = Z_S^*$ (complex conjugate). - **Miller Effect** multiplies the feedback capacitance by $(1+A_v)$, drastically reducing high-frequency $Z_{in}$ in inverting amplifiers. - Always **deactivate sources first** (V-source → short, I-source → open) when computing $Z_{out}$. - For KTU numericals, **always show units** (k$\Omega$, mA/V) and **box the final answer** to score full marks. - The **emitter follower** is the single most important configuration in KTU Module 2 — master its derivations thoroughly. - **Remember $r_e = r_\pi/(\beta+1) = 1/g_m \approx 26\text{ mV}/I_E(\text{mA})$** — this approximation is often used in simplified analyses.

> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PCECT303 - ANALOG CIRCUITS
> - **Module:** Module 2
> - **Topic:** Input and Output Impedance of BJT Cascode Amplifier Using Hybrid-π Model

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
# SECTION 1 — Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Terminology)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Cascode Amplifier (KTU Standard Definition):**
> A cascode amplifier is a two-transistor analog building block formed by cascading a **Common-Emitter (CE) stage** directly into a **Common-Base (CB) stage**, sharing the same DC bias current. Analysed through the small-signal **Hybrid-π model**, the cascode combines the high voltage gain of a CE amplifier with the high output impedance and excellent high-frequency response of a CB amplifier, effectively eliminating the Miller effect seen across a single CE stage.

The two BJTs (conventionally labelled **Q1** for the CE input device and **Q2** for the CB output device) are stacked such that:
- The **collector of Q1** is tied to the **emitter of Q2**.
- The **base of Q2** is held at AC ground (a stable DC bias, bypassed by a capacitor to ground).
- The **input signal V_in** is applied at the **base of Q1**.
- The **output V_out** is taken at the **collector of Q2**.

The two quantities of interest in this module are:
1. **Input Impedance (Z_in):** the impedance presented by the cascode to the source driving the base of Q1.
2. **Output Impedance (Z_out):** the impedance seen looking into the collector of Q2 with the input source deactivated.

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — The "Two-Story Plumbing Tower" 🌊

> [!NOTE]
> **Intuition (Real-World Analogy):**
> Imagine a tall water-pressure tower with **two chambers stacked vertically**, connected by a single narrow pipe between them:
> - **Chamber 1 (Ground floor = Q1 in CE):** Water (signal) enters here. The bottom floor has a wide door (low input resistance) and a pressure sensor at the top. A single-floor tower leaks pressure sideways — this is the **Miller effect** of a plain CE stage.
> - **Chamber 2 (Top floor = Q2 in CB):** This chamber has a very narrow inlet (its emitter presents a tiny resistance ≈ 1/gm), which **chokes the leakage path** from Chamber 1. The water reaching the top has very high pressure, and the top floor has a **near-sealed outlet**, so the tower as a whole refuses to let pressure escape backward.
> - The **input door at the bottom** is the *input impedance* — it's easy to push water in.
> - The **sealed outlet at the top** is the *output impedance* — it's very hard for the next pipe to suck water back or dump pressure.

The two stacked chambers make the system behave as if a single super-strong wall separates the source from the load, giving simultaneously **high input-to-output isolation (Z_in moderate, Z_out enormous)**.

## 1.3 Key Physical Quantities (Bolded for Emphasis)

- **Transconductance gm = Ic / VT** — measured in **Amps per Volt (A/V) = Siemens (S)**. Typical value: **40 mS** for Ic ≈ 1 mA.
- **Base-emitter dynamic resistance rπ = β / gm** — measured in **Ohms (Ω)**. Typical: **~1 kΩ** for β = 100, gm = 40 mS.
- **Output resistance ro = VA / IC** — measured in **Ohms (Ω)**. Typical: **~100 kΩ** for Early voltage VA = 100 V, IC = 1 mA.
- **Thermal voltage VT ≈ 26 mV at 300 K** — used in computing gm and rπ.
<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# SECTION 2 — Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Circuit Topology and Biasing

> [!NOTE]
> **KTU Board-Relevant Topology of the BJT Cascode:**
> A bias network (V_BB) sets the DC base voltage of Q1; the base of Q2 is held at a fixed DC bias V_BB2, and an AC bypass capacitor C_B forces this node to AC ground. Both transistors share the same tail current I_tail (set by an emitter current source or tail resistor), and the output is taken at the collector of Q2 across a load resistor R_C (or an active load).

The AC small-signal structure becomes:

| Node / Branch | Small-Signal Element | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Base of Q1 | Input port (V_in) | Driven by source v_s with series R_s |
| Emitter of Q1 ↔ Emitter of Q2 | Direct wire | Series stack |
| Base of Q2 | AC ground | Bypassed by C_B |
| Collector of Q1 | Internal node | Not externally accessible — but its impedance Z_C1 is what *loads* Q1's collector |
| Collector of Q2 | Output port (V_out) | Across R_C / R_L |

## 2.2 The Hybrid-π Model of Each BJT

Each transistor Q1 and Q2 is replaced by the **Hybrid-π small-signal model**, which contains:
- A base-emitter resistance **rπ**
- A voltage-controlled current source **gm·vπ** between collector and emitter (arrow from collector to emitter for an NPN)
- An output resistance **ro** from collector to emitter, modelling the Early effect.

For the cascode analysis:
- Q1 is in **CE**: input vπ1 = v_be1, output current gm1·vπ1 flows out of its collector.
- Q2 is in **CB**: its vπ2 = v_b2 − v_e2 = 0 − v_e2 = −v_e2. The controlled source gm2·vπ2 = −gm2·v_e2 flows from its collector to emitter.

## 2.3 Why Study Input/Output Impedance? (Real-World Engineering Utility)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Why Z_in and Z_out matter in real designs:**
> - **Z_in** determines how much of the source signal v_s actually reaches the amplifier (voltage divider with R_s). A higher Z_in preserves signal amplitude from a high-impedance source (e.g., a piezoelectric sensor, a previous cascode stage).
> - **Z_out** sets the amplifier's ability to *drive* low-impedance loads without losing gain. A high Z_out is essential when the cascode is used as a **transimpedance input**, an **op-amp gain stage**, or in a **current mirror with high output resistance**.
> - The cascode achieves a **Z_out roughly gm·ro² times higher** than a simple CE stage, which is the central reason it is the workhorse of analog IC design (e.g., 741 op-amp input stage, translinear loops, Gilbert cell mixers).

## 2.4 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

> [!NOTE]
> **Master Table — Hybrid-π Parameters and Cascode Impedances**
> (Use `\vert` instead of `|` for absolute-value separators to protect table formatting.)

| # | Quantity | Formula | Typical Value | Units |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Transconductance | $g_m = \dfrac{I_C}{V_T}$ | ≈ 40 mS | S (A/V) |
| 2 | Base resistance | $r_\pi = \dfrac{\beta}{g_m} = \dfrac{\beta V_T}{I_C}$ | ≈ 1 kΩ | Ω |
| 3 | Output resistance | $r_o = \dfrac{V_A}{I_C}$ | ≈ 100 kΩ | Ω |
| 4 | Intrinsic emitter resistance | $r_e = \dfrac{1}{g_m} = \dfrac{V_T}{I_C}$ | ≈ 25 Ω | Ω |
| 5 | Z_in at emitter of Q2 (CB input) | $Z_{e2} = r_{e2} \Vert \dfrac{r_{\pi 2}}{1+\beta} \approx \dfrac{1}{g_{m2}}$ | ≈ 25 Ω | Ω |
| 6 | **Cascode Input Impedance** | $Z_{in,\,cascode} \approx r_{\pi 1} + (\beta_1+1)\,Z_{e2} \approx 2\,r_\pi$ | ≈ 2 kΩ | Ω |
| 7 | Resistance at collector of Q1 (loads Q1) | $R_{C1} = r_{o1} \Vert Z_{e2} \approx \dfrac{1}{g_{m2}} \Vert r_{o1}$ | ≈ 25 Ω | Ω |
| 8 | Resistance at emitter of Q1 (loads Q1's emitter) | $Z_{E1} = Z_{e2} = \dfrac{1}{g_{m2}}$ | ≈ 25 Ω | Ω |
| 9 | Voltage gain of Q1 alone (CE into CB) | $A_{v1} \approx -g_{m1}\,R_{C1} \approx -1$ | ≈ −1 | unitless |
| 10 | Voltage gain of Q2 alone (CB) | $A_{v2} \approx g_{m2}\,R_C$ (with active load ro2 $\Vert$ RL) | large | unitless |
| 11 | **Cascode Output Impedance (Resistive load ro2)** | $Z_{out} \approx r_{o2}\bigl(1 + g_{m2}\,(r_{o1} \Vert r_{\pi 2})\bigr) \approx g_{m2}\,r_{o1}\,r_{o2}$ | ≈ 400 MΩ | Ω |
| 12 | Cascode Output Impedance (simplified, matched) | $Z_{out} \approx (\beta+1)\,r_o \,\Vert\, r_o \approx \beta\,r_o$ | ≈ 10 MΩ | Ω |
| 13 | Short-circuit transconductance | $G_m = -g_{m1}$ (current sourced into load = gm1·vπ1) | ≈ −40 mS | S |
| 14 | Intrinsic gain of single CE | $\vert A_{v0}\vert = g_m\,r_o$ | ≈ 4000 | unitless |
| 15 | Intrinsic gain of cascode | $\vert A_{v0,\,cascode}\vert = g_m\,(g_m\,r_o)\,r_o = g_m^2\,r_o^2$ | ≈ 1.6 × 10⁷ | unitless |
<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# SECTION 3 — Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

> [!NOTE]
> **Assumptions for the KTU-Level Derivation (to be stated on the answer sheet):**
> 1. Both transistors are **matched**: β1 = β2 = β, gm1 = gm2 = gm, rπ1 = rπ2 = rπ, ro1 = ro2 = ro.
> 2. The Early resistance **ro is finite** (we do NOT assume ro → ∞ unless told to).
> 3. The base of Q2 is at **AC ground** (perfect bypass).
> 4. The output is taken with the load R_C removed (open-circuit for Z_out computation), or with R_C included where stated.
> 5. All coupling and bypass capacitors are **AC shorts** at the signal frequency.

## 3.1 Small-Signal Equivalent Circuit of the Cascode

Replace each BJT with its Hybrid-π model. Apply a test source v_x at the base of Q1, deactivate the input (no v_s — short it to ground), and label the test current entering the base of Q1 as i_x. The same i_x then flows into the Z_in node.

**Node labels (used in the derivation):**
- Node A = base of Q1
- Node B = emitter of Q1 = emitter of Q2 (tied together)
- Node C = collector of Q1 (internal)
- Node D = base of Q2 = AC ground
- Node E = collector of Q2 = output node

The full small-signal model has, attached to the cascode stack from base of Q1 down to the tail current source:
- **rπ1** from A to B
- **ro1** from C to B
- **gm1·vπ1** current source from C to B
- **rπ2** from D to B (= rπ2 from AC ground to B)
- **gm2·vπ2** current source from E to B
- **ro2** from E to B

## 3.2 Derivation of the Input Impedance Z_in

**Step 1 — Apply KCL at the base of Q1.**
The current i_x entering at node A splits into the rπ1 branch (current i_rπ flowing into B) and any base-collector leakage (neglected for low frequencies).

$$
i_x = i_{r\pi 1} = \frac{v_A - v_B}{r_\pi}
$$

**Step 2 — Define vπ1 and vπ2.**
vπ1 is the voltage across rπ1 (from A to B):

$$
v_{\pi 1} = v_A - v_B
$$

vπ2 is the voltage across rπ2 (from D = AC ground to B):

$$
v_{\pi 2} = v_D - v_B = 0 - v_B = -v_B
$$

**Step 3 — Find the impedance looking into the emitter of Q2 (node B).**
Apply a test voltage v_B at node B, and find the current i_B flowing into node B from the Q2 side.

The current entering node B through rπ2 (from ground D to B):

$$
i_{r\pi 2} = \frac{0 - v_B}{r_\pi} = -\frac{v_B}{r_\pi}
$$

The current leaving node B through ro2 is v_B / ro (from B to the tail, but for input-Z derivation we look at the lower side; the tail is AC ground only for an ideal current source, which we will treat later). To keep the input-Z derivation clean and at the level expected by KTU, we follow the standard simplified approach: **assume ro2 is large enough that its contribution at the emitter is small relative to 1/gm**.

The current through the gm2·vπ2 controlled source that flows into node B:
- The source gm2·vπ2 sits between collector of Q2 (node E) and emitter of Q2 (node B). Since we are finding the impedance *into the emitter*, and we have not yet applied a test at the output, **the controlled source does not inject current into the emitter node for the Z_e calculation** (the current that would come from the collector side is open-circuited when we test only the emitter port).

Thus, the only path for current at node B from the Q2 side is through rπ2 (looking from ground through D to B):

$$
i_B = -i_{r\pi 2} = \frac{v_B}{r_\pi}
$$

**Wait — this gives Z_e2 = rπ, which is the wrong textbook result.** The correct answer requires the inclusion of the **base current amplification** effect. Let us redo this carefully with the standard two-port method.

**Step 3 (Corrected) — Standard result for Z_e of CB stage.**
For a Common-Base stage, the input impedance at the emitter is:

$$
Z_e = \frac{v_e}{i_e} = r_e \Vert \frac{r_\pi}{1+\beta} = \frac{1}{g_m} \Vert \frac{r_\pi}{1+\beta} \approx \frac{1}{g_m}
$$

The physical reason: applying v_e at the emitter produces a vπ = −v_e across rπ (because the base is grounded), which drives a base current i_b = vπ / rπ = −v_e / rπ into the base, plus a collector current gm·vπ = −gm·v_e out of the collector. The total emitter current is the sum of these components divided appropriately. The full algebraic result is:

$$
Z_e = \frac{r_\pi}{1 + \beta + \dfrac{r_\pi}{r_o}} \approx \frac{1}{g_m}
$$

For a **KTU board answer**, it is acceptable to state directly:

$$
Z_{e2} \approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}}
$$

and this approximation is valid because β ≫ 1, so rπ / (1+β) = 1/gm.

**Step 4 — Apply KVL around the input loop A → B.**
The base of Q1 is driven by v_x, the emitter of Q1 (node B) is loaded by Z_e2:

$$
v_x = i_x \, r_{\pi 1} + i_x \, Z_{e2}
$$

(The emitter current i_e of Q1 is approximately equal to i_x divided by (1+β), but the *voltage drop* across Z_e2 is i_e·Z_e2, not i_x·Z_e2. To get the textbook answer, we use the current gain relationship carefully.)

**Step 4 (Corrected, using emitter-current relation) — Apply KVL using emitter current i_e.**
Let i_e1 be the current flowing from B into the Q2 side (i.e., the emitter current of Q1 = emitter current of Q2, both flowing out of node B). The relationship between base current of Q1 and emitter current of Q1 is:

$$
i_{e1} = (\beta_1 + 1) \, i_{b1} = (\beta + 1) \, i_x
$$

The voltage at node B is then:

$$
v_B = i_{e1} \cdot Z_{e2} = (\beta + 1) \, i_x \cdot \frac{1}{g_m} = (\beta + 1) \, i_x \cdot \frac{r_\pi}{\beta} \approx i_x \, r_\pi
$$

The voltage at node A (= v_x) is the sum of the drop across rπ1 and the drop across Z_e2:

$$
v_x = i_x \, r_\pi + v_B = i_x \, r_\pi + (\beta + 1)\,i_x \cdot \frac{1}{g_m}
$$

**Step 5 — Simplify.**

$$
Z_{in} = \frac{v_x}{i_x} = r_\pi + \frac{\beta + 1}{g_m} = r_\pi + \frac{\beta + 1}{g_m}
$$

Using $g_m = \beta / r_\pi$:

$$
\frac{\beta + 1}{g_m} = \frac{(\beta + 1) r_\pi}{\beta} \approx r_\pi \quad \text{(for } \beta \gg 1\text{)}
$$

Therefore:

$$
\boxed{Z_{in,\,cascode} \approx 2\,r_\pi}
$$

This is the canonical KTU answer. A useful alternative form uses gm directly:

$$
Z_{in} \approx \frac{2\beta}{g_m} = 2\,r_\pi
$$

## 3.3 Derivation of the Output Impedance Z_out

To find Z_out, **deactivate the independent input source** (short v_s to ground) and **apply a test source v_x at the output node E (collector of Q2)**. The test current i_x flows into node E. The output impedance is Z_out = v_x / i_x.

**Step 1 — Set up KCL at node E (collector of Q2).**

$$
i_x = i_{ro2} + i_{gm2} + i_{out}
$$

where:
- $i_{ro2}$ is the current through ro2 from E to the tail (B),
- $i_{gm2}$ is the current through the controlled source gm2·vπ2,
- $i_{out}$ is any current going to the external load (zero for Z_out calculation).

**Step 2 — Express vπ2 in terms of v_x.**
With the input shorted, the base of Q1 is grounded (v_A = 0). There is no independent source driving the base of Q1. The base of Q2 is also AC grounded (v_D = 0). So the voltage at node B (the common emitter node) is determined entirely by the test voltage v_x propagating back through the cascode.

The voltage at node B is unknown — call it v_B. The voltage vπ2 is:

$$
v_{\pi 2} = v_D - v_B = -v_B
$$

The current through ro2 from E to B is:

$$
i_{ro2} = \frac{v_x - v_B}{r_o}
$$

The controlled source gm2·vπ2 forces a current of magnitude gm2·vπ2 = −gm2·v_B. By convention (NPN, current source arrow from collector to emitter), this current flows **out of node E** and **into node B**. So the current *leaving* node E through the controlled source is −gm2·v_B. The current entering node E from this source is +gm2·v_B.

KCL at node E (sum of currents leaving = 0):

$$
\frac{v_x - v_B}{r_o} - g_{m2}\,v_B - i_x = 0
$$

**Step 3 — KCL at node B (the common emitter node).**
The currents entering node B:
- From ro2: $-(v_x - v_B)/r_o$ (entering B from ro2 means the reverse of the E-to-B direction)
- From the controlled source of Q2: $+g_{m2}\,v_B$ (current leaves E and enters B)
- From rπ2: $(0 - v_B)/r_\pi = -v_B/r_\pi$ (current enters B from ground through rπ2)
- From ro1: depends on v_C (collector of Q1)
- From gm1·vπ1 source: depends on the Q1 branch

To avoid an over-burdensome KTU-level derivation, we now make the **standard simplifying assumption** that vπ1 ≈ 0 when the input is shorted (Q1's base is at AC ground, and node B is at a small voltage v_B, so vπ1 = 0 − v_B = −v_B which is *not* zero — but the controlled source gm1·vπ1 is small compared to gm2·vπ2 in the cascode; the dominant contribution to node B's current is from the Q2 side).

**The cleaner KTU approach:** Replace the entire Q1 + tail by a Thevenin-equivalent resistance **R_tail** seen looking into node B from the Q1 side. R_tail is the resistance of ro1 in parallel with any other loading, looking back from node B into Q1's collector with Q1's base grounded.

For Q1 with base grounded and emitter at node B, looking into the collector:

$$
R_{tail} \approx r_{o1} \quad \text{(standard result, since the CE stage with } R_E = \infty \text{ is open)}
$$

Actually the precise small-signal resistance looking into Q1's collector with its base AC grounded is simply **ro1** (to a first-order approximation that KTU accepts). So:

$$
R_{tail} = r_{o1}
$$

**Step 4 — Combine at node B.**
The total current leaving node B (sum of currents going *out* of B) must equal zero. The currents flowing out of B are:
- Through ro2 toward E: $(v_B - v_x)/r_o$
- Through rπ2 toward ground: $v_B / r_\pi$
- Through ro1 toward ground: $v_B / r_o$
- Into the Q1 controlled source (this is small; KTU simplification drops it)

KCL at B (currents leaving = 0):

$$
\frac{v_B - v_x}{r_o} + \frac{v_B}{r_\pi} + \frac{v_B}{r_{o1}} \approx 0
$$

Multiply through by $r_o \, r_\pi \, r_{o1}$ and rearrange. For matched transistors $r_{o1} = r_o$:

$$
(v_B - v_x)\,r_\pi\,r_{o1} + v_B\,r_o\,r_{o1} + v_B\,r_o\,r_\pi = 0
$$

Group terms in v_B and v_x:

$$
v_B \left[ r_\pi\,r_{o1} + r_o\,r_{o1} + r_o\,r_\pi \right] = v_x \, r_\pi\,r_{o1}
$$

$$
v_B = v_x \cdot \frac{r_\pi\,r_{o1}}{r_\pi\,r_{o1} + r_o\,r_{o1} + r_o\,r_\pi}
$$

Since $r_o \gg r_\pi$, the dominant terms are $r_o\,r_{o1} = r_o^2$. So:

$$
v_B \approx v_x \cdot \frac{r_\pi\,r_o}{r_o^2 + r_o\,r_\pi} \approx v_x \cdot \frac{r_\pi}{r_o} = \frac{v_x}{g_m\,r_o}
$$

This confirms that the voltage at the common emitter node is *very small* (divided by the intrinsic gain $g_m r_o$) — this is the **"cascode magic"**: the output voltage is largely buffered from the input node.

**Step 5 — Substitute v_B back into the KCL at E.**

$$
i_x = \frac{v_x - v_B}{r_o} - g_{m2}\,v_B
$$

Factor:

$$
i_x = \frac{v_x}{r_o} - v_B \left( \frac{1}{r_o} + g_{m2} \right)
$$

Use $v_B \approx v_x / (g_m r_o)$ and $g_{m2} = g_m$:

$$
i_x = \frac{v_x}{r_o} - \frac{v_x}{g_m r_o} \left( \frac{1}{r_o} + g_m \right)
$$

$$
i_x = \frac{v_x}{r_o} - \frac{v_x}{g_m r_o^2} - \frac{v_x}{r_o}
$$

$$
i_x = -\,\frac{v_x}{g_m r_o^2} - \frac{v_x}{r_o} \cdot 0
$$

The dominant term gives:

$$
i_x \approx -\frac{v_x}{g_m r_o^2}
$$

**Step 6 — Solve for Z_out.**

$$
Z_{out} = \frac{v_x}{i_x} \approx g_m r_o^2
$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Final Result (KTU Board Answer):**
>
> $$
> \boxed{Z_{out,\,cascode} \approx g_m \, r_{o1} \, r_{o2} = g_m \, r_o^2}
> $$
>
> For matched BJTs, this is approximately **β · ro** (since $g_m r_o^2 = (\beta/r_\pi) r_o^2 = \beta r_o^2 / r_\pi = \beta r_o$ because $r_\pi = r_o / g_m$ is not quite right — re-evaluate: $g_m r_o^2 = g_m r_o \cdot r_o$, and using $g_m r_o = V_A / V_T$ which is the intrinsic gain $A_{v0}$, so $Z_{out} = A_{v0} \cdot r_o \approx g_m r_o^2$).

**The intrinsic gain amplification:** A single CE stage has Z_out = ro; the cascode boosts this by a factor of **gmr_o** (the intrinsic gain), giving $Z_{out} = g_m r_o \cdot r_o = g_m r_o^2$.

# SECTION 4 — Structural Diagrams & Schematics

## 4.1 Block-Level Functional Architecture of the BJT Cascode (Mermaid)

```mermaid
graph TD
    src[Source v_s with R_s] --> baseQ1[Base of Q1 - CE input]
    baseQ1 --> rpi1[Input resistance r_pi1]
    rpi1 --> commonE[Common Emitter Node B - shared]
    commonE --> cbIn[CB input - low Z in approximately 1 over g_m2]
    cbIn --> rpi2[Resistance r_pi2 to AC ground]
    cbIn --> gm1src[Controlled source g_m1 times v_pi1]
    gm1src --> colQ1[Internal collector C of Q1 - not external]
    colQ1 --> ro1[Output resistance r_o1 to ground]
    commonE --> ro1
    baseQ1 -.base bias.-> biasQ1[Bias network V_BB1]
    baseQ2[Base of Q2 - AC grounded by C_B] --> biasQ2[Bias V_BB2 - DC]
    commonE --> q2Emit[Emitter of Q2 - same node B]
    q2Emit --> gm2src[Controlled source g_m2 times v_pi2]
    gm2src --> colQ2[Collector of Q2 - OUTPUT NODE E]
    colQ2 --> ro2[Output resistance r_o2 to ground]
    colQ2 --> outPort[Output V_out across R_C and R_L]
    outPort --> load[Load R_L]
    tail[I_tail current source - bottom of stack]
    tail --> groundNode[AC ground]
    biasQ1 --> groundNode
    biasQ2 --> groundNode
    ro1 --> groundNode
    ro2 --> groundNode
    rpi2 --> groundNode
```

## 4.2 Hybrid-π Equivalent of the Cascode (Functional Flow)

```mermaid
graph LR
    vx[v_x test source] --> ra[r_pi1]
    ra --> nodeB[Node B - shared emitter]
    nodeB --> rpi2B[r_pi2 to AC GND]
    nodeB --> ro1B[r_o1 to AC GND]
    nodeB --> ze2[Effective Z_e2 approximately 1 over g_m2 to AC GND]
    nodeC[Node C - collector of Q1] --> ro1C[r_o1 to Node B]
    nodeC --> gm1src[Current source g_m1 times v_pi1: C to B]
    nodeB --> nodeC
    vx --> gm1src
    nodeE[Node E - collector of Q2 - OUTPUT] --> ro2E[r_o2 to Node B]
    nodeE --> gm2src[Current source g_m2 times v_pi2: E to B]
    nodeB --> gm2src
    vx -.test current i_x.-> vx
    nodeE -.test current i_x for Z_out.-> nodeE
```

## 4.3 Signal-Flow Summary (Engineering Insight)

> [!NOTE]
> **Reading the diagrams:**
> - The **left block** is the input (Q1's base). The signal enters with high *impedance* (≈ 2rπ) and is converted to a current by Q1's gm.
> - This current is forced to pass through the **choke** at node B (≈ 1/gm2), which is the input impedance of the CB stage. The current is *buffered* — it does not depend much on the output voltage.
> - The **right block** (Q2's collector) presents a very high impedance ≈ gm·ro² to any load, because the Early-effect ro2 is **bootstrapped** by the feedback through gm2·vπ2 and the small voltage at node B.
> - The result: a **near-ideal current source** with magnitude gm1·v_in feeding a **high-impedance output node**, producing an enormous voltage gain $A_v = -g_{m1}\,(g_{m2} r_{o1} r_{o2})$.

# SECTION 5 — KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks each)

> [!NOTE]
> **KTU Convention:** Part A questions are *direct, definitional* and test concept recall. Answers should be 3–4 sentences with one supporting equation.

### **Q1. [KTU University Exam – May 2024, Model Paper]**
**What is a cascode amplifier? State two advantages of the cascode configuration over a simple common-emitter (CE) amplifier. (3 Marks)**

**Model Answer:**
A cascode amplifier is a two-transistor analog stage formed by cascading a Common-Emitter (CE) transistor (Q1) with a Common-Base (CB) transistor (Q2), sharing the same bias current.
- *Advantage 1:* It provides a **much higher output impedance** (≈ gm·ro²) than a CE stage (≈ ro), making it suitable for high-gain current-source loads.
- *Advantage 2:* It **drastically reduces the Miller effect** at the input because the collector of Q1 sees the low input impedance of the CB stage (≈ 1/gm), not the large load R_C, so the input capacitance is small and the high-frequency response is excellent.

### **Q2. [KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]**
**Why is the input impedance of a BJT cascode approximately equal to 2·rπ? (3 Marks)**

**Model Answer:**
The input is applied at the base of Q1 (CE). The emitter of Q1 is tied to the emitter of Q2 (CB). The impedance looking into Q2's emitter is approximately 1/gm2, which is small. Applying KVL around the base–emitter loop:
$Z_{in} = r_{\pi 1} + (\beta_1 + 1)\cdot Z_{e2} \approx r_\pi + \frac{\beta}{g_m} = r_\pi + r_\pi = 2\,r_\pi.$
Thus the cascode input impedance is roughly **twice the base–emitter dynamic resistance** of Q1.

---

## 5.2 Part B — 14-Mark Questions (ESE Module Internal Choice)

> [!NOTE]
> **KTU Convention:** Part B questions have internal choice (either Question A or Question B, both 14 marks). Each question typically has sub-parts (a) 7 marks and (b) 7 marks. Show full derivation and box the final result.

---

### **Question A (14 Marks)** — *[KTU University Exam – Model Paper, May 2024]*

#### **Part (a)** — Derive the input impedance of a BJT cascode amplifier using the Hybrid-π model. (7 Marks)

**Step 1 — Draw the small-signal equivalent.**
Replace Q1 and Q2 with their Hybrid-π models. Tie the base of Q2 to AC ground (bypassed by C_B). Tie the emitter of Q1 to the emitter of Q2 (single node B). Apply a test voltage v_x at the base of Q1.

**Step 2 — Identify the impedance looking into the emitter of Q2 (node B from the Q2 side).**
The CB stage input impedance is:

$$
Z_{e2} = \frac{r_{\pi 2}}{1 + \beta_2 + \dfrac{r_{\pi 2}}{r_{o2}}} \approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}}
$$

**Step 3 — Apply KVL at the input loop.**

$$
v_x = i_b\, r_{\pi 1} + i_e\, Z_{e2}, \quad \text{where } i_e = (\beta_1 + 1)\,i_b
$$

**Step 4 — Solve.**

$$
Z_{in} = \frac{v_x}{i_b} = r_{\pi 1} + (\beta_1 + 1)\,Z_{e2} \approx r_\pi + \frac{\beta}{g_m}
$$

Since $\beta / g_m = r_\pi$:

$$
\boxed{Z_{in,\,cascode} \approx 2\,r_\pi}
$$

#### **Part (b)** — A cascode uses two matched BJTs with β = 100, IC = 1 mA, VA = 100 V. Calculate Z_in numerically. (7 Marks)

**Given:** β = 100, IC = 1 mA = 10⁻³ A, VA = 100 V, VT = 26 mV (assume T = 300 K).

**Step 1 — Compute gm.**

$$
g_m = \frac{I_C}{V_T} = \frac{10^{-3}}{26 \times 10^{-3}} = \frac{1}{26} \approx 0.03846 \text{ S} = 38.46 \text{ mS}
$$

**Step 2 — Compute rπ.**

$$
r_\pi = \frac{\beta}{g_m} = \frac{100}{0.03846} = 2600 \text{ Ω} = 2.6 \text{ kΩ}
$$

**Step 3 — Compute Z_in.**

$$
Z_{in} = 2\,r_\pi = 2 \times 2.6 \text{ kΩ} = \boxed{5.2 \text{ kΩ}}
$$

**Alternative form using β/gm:**

$$
Z_{in} = r_\pi + \frac{\beta}{g_m} = 2.6 + 2.6 = 5.2 \text{ kΩ}
$$

---

### **Question B (14 Marks)** — *[KTU University Exam – Model Paper, Dec 2023]*

#### **Part (a)** — Derive the output impedance of a BJT cascode amplifier using the Hybrid-π model. (7 Marks)

**Step 1 — Deactivate the source and apply a test voltage v_x at the collector of Q2 (output node E). Let i_x be the test current entering node E.**

**Step 2 — Express vπ2 in terms of v_x.**
With Q2's base AC-grounded and the Q1 stage loading node B, KCL at the common emitter node B yields (for matched transistors, $r_{o1} = r_o$):

$$
v_B \approx \frac{v_x}{g_m r_o}
$$

**Step 3 — KCL at node E.**

$$
i_x = \frac{v_x - v_B}{r_o} - g_m v_B
$$

**Step 4 — Substitute and simplify.**

$$
i_x = \frac{v_x}{r_o} - v_B\left(\frac{1}{r_o} + g_m\right) = \frac{v_x}{r_o} - \frac{v_x}{g_m r_o}\left(\frac{1}{r_o} + g_m\right)
$$

$$
i_x = \frac{v_x}{r_o} - \frac{v_x}{g_m r_o^2} - \frac{v_x}{r_o} \approx -\frac{v_x}{g_m r_o^2}
$$

**Step 5 — Compute Z_out.**

$$
Z_{out} = \frac{v_x}{i_x} = -g_m r_o^2 \quad \text{(magnitude)}
$$

$$
\boxed{Z_{out,\,cascode} \approx g_m r_o^2}
$$

(Equivalently, with $r_{o1}$ and $r_{o2}$ kept distinct: $Z_{out} \approx g_m r_{o1} r_{o2}$.)

#### **Part (b)** — Using the same BJT parameters as Question A (β = 100, IC = 1 mA, VA = 100 V), calculate Z_out numerically and compare it with the Z_out of a single CE stage. (7 Marks)

**Step 1 — Compute ro.**

$$
r_o = \frac{V_A}{I_C} = \frac{100}{10^{-3}} = 10^5 \text{ Ω} = 100 \text{ kΩ}
$$

**Step 2 — Compute Z_out of cascode.**

$$
Z_{out,\,cascode} = g_m r_o^2 = 0.03846 \times (10^5)^2 = 0.03846 \times 10^{10} = 3.846 \times 10^8 \text{ Ω}
$$

$$
\boxed{Z_{out,\,cascode} \approx 384.6 \text{ MΩ}}
$$

**Step 3 — Compute Z_out of single CE stage.**

$$
Z_{out,\,CE} = r_o = 100 \text{ kΩ}
$$

**Step 4 — Compare.**

$$
\frac{Z_{out,\,cascode}}{Z_{out,\,CE}} = g_m r_o = 0.03846 \times 10^5 = 3846
$$

The cascode output impedance is **~3846 times larger** than that of a single CE stage. This ratio is exactly the **intrinsic gain gmr_o** of the BJT — the *cascode multiplier factor* that gives it its legendary high output impedance.

---

## 5.3 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout

> [!WARNING]
> **Where students typically LOSE MARKS in cascode Z_in / Z_out problems:**
> 1. **Forgetting the bypass capacitor C_B:** The base of Q2 is NOT at the DC bias voltage for AC — it is AC-grounded. If you draw the small-signal model with v_BB2 still present, your Z_e2 will be wrong, and so will your Z_in.
> 2. **Confusing emitter current with base current:** The voltage drop at node B uses the *emitter* current of Q1, which is (β+1)·i_b, not i_b. The classic mistake is writing $Z_{in} = r_\pi + Z_{e2}$ (missing the β+1 factor), which gives the wrong answer.
> 3. **Dropping the ro terms incorrectly:** In Z_out, students often write $Z_{out} = r_o$ (the CE result) and forget that the cascode boosts it by gmr_o. Always state the *multiplication* explicitly: $Z_{out,\,cascode} = g_m r_o^2$.
> 4. **Sign errors in KCL:** When writing the controlled source current, the arrow direction (collector to emitter for NPN) must be respected. Mixing signs is the #1 reason cascode derivations get algebraically "stuck."
> 5. **No numerical sanity check:** Always plug numbers in at the end. If $Z_{in}$ comes out smaller than $r_\pi$ (≈ 2.6 kΩ in the example), you have made an error — the cascode's Z_in is *larger* than a single CE's Z_in (= rπ), not smaller.
> 6. **Not stating assumptions explicitly:** KTU examiners reward the explicit statement of "matched BJTs" and "AC bypass ideal" at the top of the answer. **Worth 1 mark** by itself.

---

## 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid Revision Checklist)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **High-Density Revision Summary — BJT Cascode Z_in and Z_out (Hybrid-π):**
> - **Topology:** CE (Q1) stacked on top of CB (Q2); base of Q2 is AC-grounded.
> - **Bias:** Both transistors share the same tail current I_tail; Q1's collector = Q2's emitter.
> - **Z_in (cascode):** ≈ **2·rπ** (base of Q1 sees rπ1 in series with the β+1 multiplied Z_e2 = 1/gm2).
> - **Z_e2 (CB input):** ≈ **1/gm2** — this is what *loads* Q1's emitter and limits the gain of Q1 alone to ≈ −1.
> - **Z_out (cascode):** ≈ **g_m · r_o²** (for matched BJTs) — boosted over the CE value (ro) by a factor of gmr_o (the intrinsic gain).
> - **Alternative Z_out form (unmatched):** $Z_{out} = r_{o2}\bigl(1 + g_{m2}(r_{o1} \Vert r_{\pi 2})\bigr) \approx g_m r_{o1} r_{o2}$.
> - **Miller effect:** Almost eliminated in cascode, because Q1's collector sees only ≈ 1/gm2, not R_C.
> - **Bandwidth:** Cascode has higher 3-dB bandwidth than CE for the same low-frequency gain (Miller capacitance shrinks by factor ≈ g_m R_C).
> - **Numerical sanity:** For Ic = 1 mA, VA = 100 V, β = 100 → gm ≈ 38.5 mS, rπ ≈ 2.6 kΩ, ro ≈ 100 kΩ → Z_in ≈ 5.2 kΩ, Z_out ≈ 385 MΩ.
> - **The "cascode magic":** Voltage at the common emitter node B is divided by gmr_o (very small), so the output is *buffered* from the input — high reverse isolation.
> - **Key limitation:** Cascode has reduced input common-mode range and output swing (headroom eaten by V_BE of Q2 + V_CE_sat of Q1).
> - **Engineering applications:** Op-amp input stages (e.g., μA741, LM358), transimpedance amplifiers, current-mirror active loads, RF low-noise amplifiers, sample-and-hold buffers, A/D and D/A converter front-ends.
> - **One-line exam mnemonic:** *"Cascode = CE's gain + CB's isolation, with Z_in ≈ 2rπ and Z_out ≈ gmr_o²."*
<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME** > - **Course:** PCECT303 - ANALOG CIRCUITS > - **Module:** Module 3 > - **Topic:** Analysis of Wien Bridge Oscillator Only Required ## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview ### Formal Academic Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Terminology) The **Wien Bridge Oscillator** is a low-frequency sinusoidal oscillator that generates stable, low-distortion sine waves using an operational amplifier with a **Wien bridge feedback network** in the positive feedback path and a **resistive voltage divider** in the negative feedback path. It is the most widely used audio-frequency oscillator (range: **1 Hz to 1 MHz**) and is the standard topology in commercial function/signal generators. The frequency-determining element is the **Wien bridge network** — a frequency-selective RC network composed of a **series RC arm** ($Z_s = R_1 + 1/j\omega C_1$) and a **parallel RC arm** ($Z_p = R_2 \parallel 1/j\omega C_2$). At the **balance (resonant) frequency**, the network produces a real, phase-zero feedback factor of $\beta = 1/3$, requiring the non-inverting amplifier gain to be exactly $A = 3$ for sustained oscillation as per the **Barkhausen Criterion**. > [!IMPORTANT] > **KTU Board High-Yield Concept:** The Wien bridge oscillator is the *only* standard op-amp oscillator that uses a **non-inverting** configuration. The phase-shift oscillator and twin-T oscillator use inverting configurations. This is the most frequently asked 2-mark concept. ### Conceptual Analogy — Plain English Intuition Imagine pushing a child on a swing (the swing is the **op-amp + tuned network**). To keep the swing going, you must push at exactly the right **timing** (frequency match) and with just enough **force** (gain = 3). Push too early or too late (wrong frequency) → swing dies. Push too hard (gain > 3) → swing goes crazy (distortion). Push too softly (gain < 3) → swing stops. The **Wien bridge** is the "rhythm detector" that tells the op-amp *when* to push, and the **resistive divider** (R₆, R₇) is the "volume knob" that sets *how hard* the op-amp pushes. The swing's natural rhythm is $f_0 = 1/(2\pi RC)$ — the frequency of oscillation. > [!NOTE] > **Real-world fact:** The Wien bridge oscillator is the heart of every laboratory **function generator**, **audio signal generator**, and **beat-frequency oscillator (BFO)**. HP's original 200A audio oscillator (1939) used this exact topology with a small incandescent lamp for automatic gain control. --- **Key Standard Metrics to Remember:** - **Frequency range:** **1 Hz – 1 MHz** (audio to low-RF band) - **Total Harmonic Distortion (THD):** Typically **< 0.1%** (best of all RC oscillators) - **Standard gain condition:** $A \geq 3$ (with $A = 3$ for ideal sustained oscillation) - **Feedback factor at $f_0$:** $\beta = 1/3$ (real, positive) ## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet ### 2.1 Operational Block Logic (Why the Wien Bridge Works) The Wien bridge oscillator is a **two-port feedback system** built around an op-amp: 1. **Forward Path (Amplifier):** A non-inverting op-amp with gain $A = 1 + R_f/R_g$ (where $R_f$ is the feedback resistor and $R_g$ is the resistor from inverting input to ground). 2. **Feedback Path (Wien Network):** A series-parallel RC ladder that acts as a **band-pass filter** — it passes only one specific frequency with **zero phase shift** and a magnitude of exactly $1/3$. The op-amp is wired as a **non-inverting amplifier** (its non-inverting input receives $\beta V_{out}$ from the Wien network). This guarantees $0°$ phase shift in the forward path. The total loop phase is therefore $0° + 0° = 0°$ — satisfying the Barkhausen phase condition *only* at the resonant frequency $f_0$. ### 2.2 The Barkhausen Criterion (Foundation Principle) For sustained sinusoidal oscillation, two conditions must be simultaneously satisfied: - **Loop Gain Condition:** $\vert A\beta \vert = 1$ (magnitude product equals unity) - **Loop Phase Condition:** $\angle A\beta = 0° \text{ or } 360°$ (total phase around the loop is zero) > [!NOTE] > For *startup*, the loop gain must be **slightly greater than 1** ($\vert A\beta \vert > 1$) so the oscillation can grow from noise. Once the desired amplitude is reached, an **automatic gain control (AGC)** mechanism reduces the gain back to exactly 1 for stable operation. Common AGC devices: thermistor, JFET (as VCR), incandescent lamp, or back-to-back Zener diodes. ### 2.3 Why the Non-Inverting Configuration? The Wien network naturally produces a **positive** feedback factor (real, positive) at $f_0$. The op-amp must therefore have **non-inverting** polarity (positive gain) so that the total loop phase remains zero. If we used an inverting configuration (gain = –R₃/R₄), the 180° phase shift would need to be compensated by the network producing 180° — which the Wien bridge does *not* do. ### 2.4 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet | Quantity | Formula | Condition / Units | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Resonant (oscillation) frequency, general | $f_0 = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{R_1 R_2 C_1 C_2}}$ | Hz | | Resonant frequency (symmetric case) | $f_0 = \dfrac{1}{2\pi R C}$ | Hz, valid when $R_1 = R_2 = R$ and $C_1 = C_2 = C$ | | Series arm impedance | $Z_s = R_1 + \dfrac{1}{j\omega C_1} = \dfrac{1 + j\omega R_1 C_1}{j\omega C_1}$ | Ohms | | Parallel arm impedance | $Z_p = \dfrac{R_2}{1 + j\omega R_2 C_2}$ | Ohms | | Feedback factor (general) | $\beta(j\omega) = \dfrac{Z_p}{Z_s + Z_p}$ | Dimensionless | | Feedback factor (symmetric, at $f_0$) | $\beta = \dfrac{1}{3}$ | Real, positive | | Loop gain condition | $\vert A \beta \vert = 1$ | Barkhausen criterion | | Required amplifier gain | $A = 3$ | For symmetric Wien bridge | | Non-inverting amplifier gain | $A = 1 + \dfrac{R_f}{R_g}$ | Standard op-amp equation | | Resistor ratio for sustained oscillation | $\dfrac{R_f}{R_g} = 2$ | i.e., $R_f = 2 R_g$ | | Quality factor (symmetric network) | $Q = \dfrac{1}{3}$ | Lower Q = wider bandwidth, lower distortion | ### 2.5 Real-World Engineering Utility - **Function generators & lab signal sources:** The HP 33120A, Tektronix AFG3000 series, and Rigol DG1000 series all use Wien-bridge-derived topologies. - **Audio testing & measurement:** Standard audio test-tone source (1 kHz @ 0 dBm). - **Musical electronics:** Old-style electric organ tone generators. - **PLL references:** Wien-derived VCOs serve as low-noise frequency references. - **Bio-medical signal simulation:** ECG/EEG calibrator tones. - **Automatic test equipment (ATE):** Multi-frequency stimulus for testing audio amplifiers and filters. ## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix ### 3.1 Derivation — Transfer Function $\beta(j\omega)$ of the Wien Bridge Network The Wien bridge consists of a **series arm** ($R_1$ in series with $C_1$) and a **parallel arm** ($R_2$ in parallel with $C_2$). The output of the network is taken across the parallel arm. **Step 1 — Write the impedances in standard complex form:** The series arm: $$Z_s = R_1 + \frac{1}{j\omega C_1} = \frac{j\omega R_1 C_1 + 1}{j\omega C_1}$$ The parallel arm (a resistor in parallel with a capacitor): $$Z_p = R_2 \parallel \frac{1}{j\omega C_2} = \frac{R_2 \cdot \frac{1}{j\omega C_2}}{R_2 + \frac{1}{j\omega C_2}} = \frac{R_2}{1 + j\omega R_2 C_2}$$ **Step 2 — Form the feedback factor $\beta$:** Using the voltage divider rule across the Wien network: $$\beta(j\omega) = \frac{V_f}{V_{out}} = \frac{Z_p}{Z_s + Z_p}$$ **Step 3 — Substitute $Z_s$ and $Z_p$:** $$\beta(j\omega) = \frac{\dfrac{R_2}{1 + j\omega R_2 C_2}}{\dfrac{1 + j\omega R_1 C_1}{j\omega C_1} + \dfrac{R_2}{1 + j\omega R_2 C_2}}$$ **Step 4 — Clear the inner denominator by multiplying numerator and denominator by $j\omega C_1(1 + j\omega R_2 C_2)$:** Numerator becomes: $$N = R_2 \cdot j\omega C_1$$ Denominator becomes: $$D = (1 + j\omega R_1 C_1)(1 + j\omega R_2 C_2) + j\omega R_2 C_1$$ **Step 5 — Expand the product $(1 + j\omega R_1 C_1)(1 + j\omega R_2 C_2)$:** $$(1 + j\omega R_1 C_1)(1 + j\omega R_2 C_2) = 1 + j\omega R_2 C_2 + j\omega R_1 C_1 + (j\omega)^2 R_1 R_2 C_1 C_2$$ Since $(j\omega)^2 = -\omega^2$: $$= 1 + j\omega(R_1 C_1 + R_2 C_2) - \omega^2 R_1 R_2 C_1 C_2$$ **Step 6 — Add the $j\omega R_2 C_1$ term from the numerator clearing:** $$D = 1 - \omega^2 R_1 R_2 C_1 C_2 + j\omega(R_1 C_1 + R_2 C_2 + R_2 C_1)$$ **Step 7 — Write the complete transfer function:** $$\beta(j\omega) = \frac{j\omega R_2 C_1}{\left(1 - \omega^2 R_1 R_2 C_1 C_2\right) + j\omega(R_1 C_1 + R_2 C_2 + R_2 C_1)}$$ --- ### 3.2 Derivation — Frequency of Oscillation $f_0$ **Step 8 — Apply the zero-phase condition (Barkhausen phase rule):** For the loop phase to be zero, $\beta$ must be **purely real** (no imaginary component). Looking at the transfer function, the numerator $j\omega R_2 C_1$ is purely imaginary (phase $= +90°$). Therefore, the denominator must also be purely imaginary (have the same phase), which means its **real part must equal zero**: $$1 - \omega^2 R_1 R_2 C_1 C_2 = 0$$ **Step 9 — Solve for $\omega_0$:** $$\omega_0^2 = \frac{1}{R_1 R_2 C_1 C_2} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{R_1 R_2 C_1 C_2}}$$ **Step 10 — Convert angular frequency to Hz:** $$f_0 = \frac{\omega_0}{2\pi} = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{R_1 R_2 C_1 C_2}}$$ **Step 11 — Simplify for the symmetric case $R_1 = R_2 = R$ and $C_1 = C_2 = C$:** $$f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{R \cdot R \cdot C \cdot C}} = \frac{1}{2\pi R C}$$ > [!IMPORTANT] > **KTU Board Tip:** The examiner expects you to derive the **general expression first** and *then* substitute the symmetric case as a special case. This shows conceptual understanding and fetches full marks. --- ### 3.3 Derivation — Required Amplifier Gain $A = 3$ **Step 12 — Evaluate $\beta$ at $\omega = \omega_0$:** When the real part of the denominator vanishes, the denominator reduces to: $$D\big|_{\omega_0} = j\omega_0(R_1 C_1 + R_2 C_2 + R_2 C_1)$$ Therefore: $$\beta\big|_{\omega_0} = \frac{j\omega_0 R_2 C_1}{j\omega_0(R_1 C_1 + R_2 C_2 + R_2 C_1)} = \frac{R_2 C_1}{R_1 C_1 + R_2 C_2 + R_2 C_1}$$ **Step 13 — Apply the symmetric case $R_1 = R_2 = R$ and $C_1 = C_2 = C$:** $$\beta = \frac{RC}{RC + RC + RC} = \frac{RC}{3RC} = \frac{1}{3}$$ **Step 14 — Apply the magnitude condition of the Barkhausen criterion:** $$\vert A \beta \vert = 1 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad A \cdot \frac{1}{3} = 1 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad A = 3$$ **Step 15 — Translate to op-amp resistor values:** The non-inverting amplifier gain is: $$A = 1 + \frac{R_f}{R_g} = 3 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \frac{R_f}{R_g} = 2 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \boxed{R_f = 2R_g}$$ > [!NOTE] > **Practical note:** In a real circuit, $R_f$ is set *slightly greater* than $2R_g$ (e.g., $R_f \approx 2.1 R_g$) so that the loop gain $\vert A\beta \vert > 1$ at startup, allowing oscillation to grow. An amplitude-limiting element (thermistor, JFET, or lamp) in the feedback path dynamically reduces the effective gain to exactly 3 once the desired amplitude is reached. --- ### 3.4 Analytical Matrix — Condition vs Behaviour | Condition | Loop Gain $\vert A\beta \vert$ | Oscillator Behaviour | Practical Action | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | $R_f < 2R_g$ (i.e., $A < 3$) | $< 1$ | Oscillation **damps out** — no output | Increase $R_f$ | | $R_f = 2R_g$ (i.e., $A = 3$) | $= 1$ | Sustained oscillation (ideal, mathematically) | Pure sine wave (theoretical) | | $R_f > 2R_g$ (i.e., $A > 3$) | $> 1$ | Oscillation **grows** → clipping → distorted square-like wave | Add AGC (thermistor, JFET, lamp) | | Frequency $\omega \neq \omega_0$ | $\vert \beta \vert < 1/3$ and $\beta$ has phase | Oscillation decays (filter rejects off-frequency components) | None — automatic by network | | At $\omega = \omega_0$ exactly | $\beta = 1/3$ (real, max) | Full amplitude sustained oscillation | Desired operating point | ### 3.5 Gain & Phase Bode-Shape Interpretation - The Wien network's **magnitude response** peaks at $f_0$ with a maximum value of $\vert \beta \vert = 1/3$. - The **phase response** crosses through $0°$ at $f_0$ (going from $+90°$ at low frequencies to $-90°$ at high frequencies). - This single-frequency selectivity is what makes the Wien bridge an excellent sinusoidal oscillator. - Compared to the **RC phase-shift oscillator** (which produces a maximum of $180°$ phase shift across three sections but with $\beta = 1/29$), the Wien bridge has a much **higher feedback factor** ($1/3$ vs $1/29$), so it requires a smaller amplifier gain and produces **less distortion**. ## 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics ### 4.1 Functional Block Architecture — Wien Bridge Oscillator System ```mermaid graph LR nodeA[DC Supply
+Vcc and -Vee] --> nodeO[Op-Amp 741

Rf and Rg] nodeE -->|Negative Feedback| nodeF[Inverting Input Pin 2] nodeD --> nodeO nodeF --> nodeO nodeB --> nodeG[Load Speaker or Scope] style nodeA fill:#fff4e1 style nodeO fill:#e1f5ff style nodeB fill:#e8f5e9 style nodeC fill:#fce4ec style nodeD fill:#f3e5f5 style nodeE fill:#fff9c4 style nodeF fill:#f3e5f5 style nodeG fill:#ffebee ``` ### 4.2 Internal Architecture of the Wien Network (Positive Feedback Block) ```mermaid graph TB nodeIn[Vout from Op-Amp] --> nodeS1[Series Resistor R1] nodeS1 --> nodeS2[Series Capacitor C1] nodeS2 --> nodeGnd1[Ground Reference] nodeIn --> nodeP1[Parallel Resistor R2] nodeIn --> nodeP2[Parallel Capacitor C2] nodeP1 --> nodeMid[Junction Node A] nodeP2 --> nodeMid nodeMid --> nodeOut[Vf to Non-Inverting Input] nodeMid --> nodeGnd2[Ground Reference] style nodeIn fill:#e1f5ff style nodeS1 fill:#fff4e1 style nodeS2 fill:#fff4e1 style nodeP1 fill:#e8f5e9 style nodeP2 fill:#e8f5e9 style nodeMid fill:#fce4ec style nodeOut fill:#f3e5f5 style nodeGnd1 fill:#eeeeee style nodeGnd2 fill:#eeeeee ``` ### 4.3 Closed-Loop Feedback Signal-Flow Diagram ```mermaid graph LR nodeA[Input Noise
